meta.title: Design review: international money transfer (iOS)
meta.scope: Amount entry and review screens of the send-money flow, from two screenshots and a journey description.

input_context.audience: Adults sending money abroad, mostly occasional users
goals: Reduce support contacts about unexpected fees

coverage.limitation: Only two screens of one flow were supplied, so app-wide structure cannot be judged.
No component library or token data was supplied; two screens are too few to judge consistency.

executive_summary.verdict: The flow is short and the amount screen is clear, but the review screen hides the information users most need before committing money: the fee and the delivery time. Fixing that is the highest-value change and directly supports the goal of fewer fee-related support contacts.
strengths: The amount screen has one clear task, a large numeric input and a visible exchange rate.
The recipient is shown with name and last digits of the account, which supports error checking.

findings.title: Fee and delivery time are shown only in small grey text below the Confirm button

evidence.region: below the Confirm button, bottom of screen
evidence.observation: The line 'Fee $4.99 - arrives in 1-2 days' sits under the Confirm button in small grey text, while the summary card above lists only amount and recipient.

findings.impact: Users commit money before seeing the cost, which risks surprise at statement time and support contacts about fees.
findings.recommendation: Move fee, total debited and delivery estimate into the summary card above the button, as labelled rows, and show the total the sender pays.
findings.rationale: People decide on the confirmation screen using what is inside the summary; costs placed after the action read as fine print and undermine trust in a money product.

findings.title: Helper and rate text is low-contrast grey at a small size

evidence.region: exchange-rate line under the amount field
evidence.observation: The rate line is light grey on a white background at roughly 11pt.

findings.impact: Users with low vision or in bright light may miss the rate, which is the information needed to judge the transfer.
findings.recommendation: Darken the rate text to a measured contrast of at least 4.5:1 and raise it to at least 13pt, then verify with a contrast tool on the real colour values.
findings.rationale: The estimate comes from a compressed screenshot, so the exact ratio needs measuring, but the visual weight is low enough that the key rate is easy to overlook.

findings.title: Confirm and Cancel use the same filled button style

evidence.observation: Confirm and Cancel are both full-width filled buttons of the same height; only the colour differs, and Cancel is a saturated red.

findings.impact: A saturated red button draws as much attention as the primary action and invites an accidental tap on the wrong choice.
findings.recommendation: Keep Confirm as the single filled button and turn Cancel into a text button or a back link, using a neutral colour.
findings.rationale: One dominant action per screen makes the next step obvious; destructive-looking styling on a harmless exit adds noise and anxiety.

findings.title: Recipient section uses the internal term 'Beneficiary'

evidence.observation: The heading reads 'Beneficiary details', while the amount screen calls the same person 'Recipient'.

findings.impact: The term shifts mid-flow and is banking jargon that occasional senders may not map to the person they chose.
findings.recommendation: Use 'Recipient' on both screens and reserve any legal term for the receipt.
findings.rationale: Consistent plain words reduce the chance that users stop to wonder whether this is a different person or step.

assumptions: The journey description is accurate: there are no further screens between review and submission.
open_questions: Is the fee dynamic per corridor? If so, the review screen must show the final fee, not an estimate.
Is there analytics on drop-off at the review screen to confirm the fee concern?

dimensions.rationale: Not assessed: Only two screens of one flow were supplied, so app-wide structure cannot be judged.
No findings in this dimension within the assessed scope.
Not assessed: No component library or token data was supplied; two screens are too few to judge consistency.

annotations.label: Fee and delivery time shown after the button

concepts.title: Cost-first review card
concepts.description: Replace the thin summary with a card that lists amount, fee, total debited, recipient gets and arrival date as labelled rows, followed by one primary Confirm button with a text-only Cancel.
concepts.tradeoffs: The card is taller, so on small phones the button may sit just below the fold; a sticky footer button mitigates this.
concepts.expected_impact: Fewer fee surprises and fewer cancellations caused by misreading the button pair; testable by comparing fee-related support contacts.

redesign_specs.title: Review screen summary and actions
redesign_specs.summary: Show all costs in the summary above the action and make Confirm the only prominent button.
layout: Summary card at the top with five labelled rows
Sticky footer containing the Confirm button and a text Cancel link beneath it

components.name: SummaryRow
components.change: Label left, value right, total row in semibold

components.name: Button/Primary
components.change: Single filled button, full width, 52pt high

states.name: Loading fee
states.behaviour: Show skeleton rows and disable Confirm until the final fee is returned

accessibility_notes: Value text at least 16pt and contrast verified on real colour values
acceptance_criteria: Fee, total debited and arrival date are visible without scrolling on a 390x844 screen before the Confirm button
Cancel is not a filled button

limitations: Reviewed from two static screenshots; interaction states, error handling and animations were not visible.
Contrast values are estimated from screenshots and must be measured on the source colours.
